sections.heading: Point estimates for the mean and variance

questions.q: A sample of 8 measurements has values $12, 15, 11, 14, 13, 16, 12, 15$. Find the unbiased point estimate of the population mean.
questions.answer: $\bar{x}=(12+15+11+14+13+16+12+15)/8=108/8=13.5$. This sample mean is itself the unbiased estimate of the population mean $\mu$.

questions.q: Explain why the unbiased estimator of population variance divides the sum of squared deviations by $n-1$ rather than $n$, using the formula $s^2=1/(n-1)\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2$.
questions.answer: Dividing by $n$ would systematically underestimate the true population variance on average, because $\bar{x}$ is calculated FROM the same sample, making the sample's squared deviations from $\bar{x}$ slightly smaller than deviations from the true (unknown) population mean $\mu$ would be. Dividing by $n-1$ (the degrees of freedom) corrects this bias, making $s^2$ an unbiased estimator of $\sigma^2$.

questions.q: For the sample $4,7,9,6,9$, find the unbiased estimate of the population variance.

sections.heading: Constructing a confidence interval for the mean

questions.q: A sample of $n=36$ has mean $\bar{x}=52$ and population standard deviation $\sigma=6$ (known). Construct a 95% confidence interval for the population mean, using $z^*=1.96$.
questions.answer: Standard error: $\sigma/(\sqrt{n})=6/(\sqrt{36})=1$. Margin of error: $1.96(1)=1.96$. Confidence interval: $52\pm1.96$, or $(50.04,53.96)$.

questions.q: A sample of $n=25$ has mean $\bar{x}=80$ and unbiased sample standard deviation $s=10$ (population standard deviation unknown, so a $t$-distribution is used). Construct a 90% confidence interval, using $t^*\approx1.711$ (with $df=24$).
questions.answer: Standard error: $s/(\sqrt{n})=10/(\sqrt{25})=2$. Margin of error: $1.711(2)=3.422$. Confidence interval: $80\pm3.422$, or approximately $(76.58,83.42)$.

questions.q: A 95% confidence interval for a population mean is calculated as $(48.2,55.8)$. State the correct interpretation of this interval, and identify a common misinterpretation to avoid.
questions.answer: Correct interpretation: if this sampling and interval-construction process were repeated many times, approximately 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the true population mean. A common misinterpretation to avoid: it is NOT correct to say there is a 95% probability that the true mean lies within this specific interval — the true mean is a fixed (though unknown) value, not a random variable, so once the interval is calculated it either does or does not contain it.

questions.q: A researcher wants to halve the margin of error of a confidence interval for the mean, keeping the confidence level and $\sigma$ fixed. Explain how the required sample size $n$ must change, using the formula for margin of error $E=z^*\sigma/(\sqrt{n})$.
questions.answer: Since $E$ is inversely proportional to $\sqrt{n}$, halving $E$ requires $\sqrt{n}$ to double, which means $n$ itself must be multiplied by $4$ (quadrupled) — a direct consequence of the square-root relationship between sample size and margin of error.

questions.q: A researcher wants a 95% confidence interval for a population mean with a margin of error no larger than $2$, given a known population standard deviation $\sigma=9$. Find the minimum required sample size, using $z^*=1.96$ and rounding up to the nearest whole number.
questions.answer: $E=z^*\sigma/\sqrt{n}$, so $n=(z^*\sigma/E)^2=(1.96(9)/2)^2=(8.82)^2\approx77.79$. Rounding up (sample size must always round up to guarantee the target margin of error): $n=78$.

questions.q: A survey of 200 randomly selected voters finds that 120 support a proposal. Construct a 95% confidence interval for the true population proportion, using $\hat{p}\pm z^*\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n}$ with $z^*=1.96$.
questions.answer: $\hat{p}=120/200=0.6$. Standard error: $\sqrt{0.6(0.4)/200}=\sqrt{0.0012}\approx0.0346$. Margin of error: $1.96(0.0346)\approx0.0679$. Confidence interval: $0.6\pm0.0679$, or approximately $(0.532,0.668)$.

sections.heading: Comparing pooled vs. unbiased variance estimates

questions.q: Two independent samples give unbiased variance estimates $s_1^2=16$ (from $n_1=10$) and $s_2^2=25$ (from $n_2=15$). Find the pooled variance estimate, using $s_p^2=((n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2)/(n_1+n_2-2)$.

sections.heading: Effect of confidence level on interval width

questions.q: Explain why a 99% confidence interval is always wider than a 95% confidence interval for the same sample data, referencing the critical value $z^*$ used in each.
questions.answer: A higher confidence level requires a larger critical value $z^*$ (approximately $2.576$ for 99% versus $1.96$ for 95%), since capturing the true parameter with greater certainty requires a wider net. Since the margin of error $E=z^*\sigma/(\sqrt{n})$ is directly proportional to $z^*$, a larger $z^*$ produces a wider confidence interval for the same sample data — there is an inherent tradeoff between confidence level and precision.

sections.heading: Constructing a confidence interval for a difference of means

questions.q: Two independent samples give $\bar{x}_1=45$ (with $n_1=40$, $\sigma_1=8$) and $\bar{x}_2=40$ (with $n_2=50$, $\sigma_2=6$). Construct a 95% confidence interval for $\mu_1-\mu_2$, using $z^*=1.96$ and the standard error formula $\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1+\sigma_2^2/n_2}$.
questions.answer: Point estimate: $\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2=45-40=5$. Standard error: $\sqrt{64/40+36/50}=\sqrt{1.6+0.72}=\sqrt{2.32}\approx1.523$. Margin of error: $1.96(1.523)\approx2.99$. Confidence interval: $5\pm2.99$, or approximately $(2.01,7.99)$.

sections.heading: Assessing whether a claimed population mean is plausible

questions.q: A machine is supposed to fill bottles with $500$ml of liquid. A sample of $n=30$ bottles has mean $\bar{x}=497$ml and sample standard deviation $s=8$ml. Construct a 95% confidence interval for the true mean fill volume (using $z^*\approx1.96$ as an approximation for the $t$-distribution with $df=29$), and use it to comment on whether the machine's target of $500$ml is plausible.
questions.answer: Standard error: $s/(\sqrt{n})=8/(\sqrt{30})\approx1.461$. Margin of error: $1.96(1.461)\approx2.86$. Confidence interval: $497\pm2.86$, or approximately $(494.14,499.86)$. Since the target value of $500$ml lies outside this confidence interval, there is evidence at the 95% confidence level that the machine's true mean fill volume is below the target of $500$ml.

questions.q: Explain why increasing the sample size $n$, while keeping everything else fixed, makes a confidence interval narrower, referencing the standard error formula $\sigma/(\sqrt{n})$.
questions.answer: The standard error $\sigma/(\sqrt{n})$ decreases as $n$ increases, since $n$ appears in the denominator under a square root. A smaller standard error directly produces a smaller margin of error $E=z^*\sigma/(\sqrt{n})$, and hence a narrower confidence interval — intuitively, a larger sample gives a more precise (less variable) estimate of the population mean.

questions.q: Two independent 95% confidence intervals for population means are $(10,14)$ and $(13,17)$. Explain what can and cannot be concluded about whether the two population means are different, given that the intervals overlap.
questions.answer: Since the two confidence intervals overlap (both contain values between $13$ and $14$), it is plausible that the two population means could be equal, so we cannot conclude at the 95% confidence level that the means are different. However, overlapping confidence intervals do not definitively prove the means are equal either — a formal hypothesis test comparing the two means directly (e.g. a two-sample $t$-test) would be needed to draw a rigorous conclusion, since the overlap-based reasoning is only an informal, conservative check.

questions.q: A student proposes using the sample maximum as an estimator for the population mean. Explain why this estimator is biased.
questions.answer: The sample maximum systematically overestimates the population mean, since it will almost always exceed the centre of the distribution (assuming the distribution has some spread), so its expected value is greater than $\mu$. An unbiased estimator must have an expected value exactly equal to the parameter being estimated; since $E(\text{sample max})>\mu$ in general, the sample maximum is a biased estimator of the mean.

sections.heading: Sensitivity of the mean to outliers

questions.q: A sample of 5 values is $4,5,6,7,50$, where the last value is a data-entry error that should have been $5$. Find the unbiased point estimate of the mean with and without correcting the error, and comment on how sensitive this estimator is to outliers.
questions.answer: With the error: mean $=(4+5+6+7+50)/5=72/5=14.4$. Corrected: mean $=(4+5+6+7+5)/5=27/5=5.4$. A single incorrect value changes the estimate from $5.4$ to $14.4$ — more than double — showing that the sample mean is highly sensitive to outliers, since every value contributes directly and equally to the sum used to compute it.

questions.q: Explain how a one-sided (upper) confidence bound differs from a standard two-sided confidence interval, and give its general form using $z^*$.
questions.answer: A two-sided confidence interval splits the margin of error evenly above and below the point estimate: $\bar{x}\pm z^*\sigma/\sqrt{n}$. A one-sided upper confidence bound instead reports only an upper limit, $\bar{x}+z^*\sigma/\sqrt{n}$, using a smaller (one-tailed) critical value $z^*$ for the same overall confidence level, since all of the tail probability is placed on one side rather than split between two.

sections.heading: Properties of the sample mean as an estimator

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the sample mean $\bar{x}$ as an estimator of the population mean $\mu$ is correct?
choices: $\bar{x}$ is unbiased, since $E(\bar{x})=\mu$ for any sample size.
$\bar{x}$ is biased for small sample sizes but becomes unbiased as $n\to\infty$.
$\bar{x}$ is unbiased only when the population is normally distributed.
$\bar{x}$ is biased because it is calculated from a subset of the population.
questions.answer: The sample mean is unbiased for any sample size and for any population distribution (not just normal), because $E(\bar{x})=\mu$ always holds by the linearity of expectation — this is a general property of $\bar{x}$, not something that only emerges asymptotically or under normality.
